newsitem.title: INDIA: India cites six near-midair collisions.
newsitem.headline: India cites six near-midair collisions.

text.p: Planes flying over Indian skies nearly collided six times in the three months after the world's worst mid-air accident in November in which 349 people died, Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim said on Tuesday.

"Six 'air-miss' incidents have been reported in the Indian skies since the mid-air collision between two planes on 12.11.96," Ibrahim said in a written statement presented in the Rajya Sabha, the upper house of parliament.
On November 12, a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 freighter collided about 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi.
There were no survivors among the 312 people aboard the Saudi jumbo and the 37 on the Kazakh plane.
Ibrahim said Dutch airline flight KLM 807 and Emirates Airlines flight UAE 082 nearly collided on November 16.
There were five cases of near-collision in January, including two involving foreign airlines, the minister said.
An Indian Airlines Airbus 320 and an Indian Air Force Boeing 737 narrowly missed each other in mid-air on January 3, he said.
Another Indian Airlines airplane and an Air-India nearly collided on January 4. Two domestic flights, Alliance Air's Flight CD 257 and Jet Air's flight 612, narrowly missed each other on January 9.

Both Indian Airlines and Air-India are state owned. Indian Airlines is the domestic carrier, while Air-India is the international airline. Alliance is a subsidiary of Indian Airlines, and Jet Air is privately owned.
Kuwait Airways' flight KAC 365 and Air Lanka's flight ALK 505 nearly collided on January 11, the statement said.
It added that Malaysian Airlines flight MAS 6125 and Singapore Airlines flight SIA 422 nearly missed each other on January 17.

The government was taking several measures, including modernisation of air-traffic services, proper maintainence of communication equipments and training of professionals to avoid mid-air collisions, the minister's statement said.
The November mid-air collision focused world attention on flight safety in India, where economic growth has spurred tourism, putting pressure on outdated air-traffic systems.
A multi-million-dollar plan to modernise radar and communications systems at major airports has fallen well behind schedule.

Due to be operational six months ago, a state-of-the-art air traffic control system built by Raytheon Co of the United States has been held up by technical glitches. In November, Raytheon had said the system would soon be ready for use.
India needs huge doses of private investment to build vital airport infrastructure and spruce up flight safety, aviation experts say.
India dismantled a state aviation monopoly as part of a series of sweeping economic reforms in 1991, opening its skies to a dozen private airlines.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet in January allowed foreign investors to take stakes of up to 40 percent in domestic airlines but said foreign airlines cannot directly buy stakes in domestic airlines.
India has five international and 87 domestic airports. The Delhi and Bombay airports handle nearly half the total traffic.
Indian airports handled 23 million passengers in fiscal year 1993/94 to end-March. That figure is estimated to rise to 110 million by the year 2011.
